qs.q: A patient with known IgA deficiency develops urticaria, angioedema, stridor, and severe hypotension shortly after the start of a blood transfusion. What is the most important first-line drug treatment?
qs.e: This patient is experiencing life-threatening anaphylaxis due to anti-IgA antibodies reacting with donor blood, requiring immediate administration of intramuscular adrenaline. Furosemide is used for fluid overload reactions like TACO rather than IgA-mediated anaphylactic shock.

qs.q: A patient presents with urticaria and angioedema shortly after receiving a specific local anesthetic. The reaction is identified as anaphylactoid rather than a true IgE-mediated allergy. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of this reaction?
o: Non-IgE mediated direct mast cell activation
Immune complex deposition in small vessels
qs.e: Anaphylactoid reactions are explicitly defined in the notes as non-IgE mediated, often resulting from agents like local anesthetics. True allergic reactions are IgE mediated.

qs.q: A patient with hereditary angioedema experiences recurrent episodes of severe swelling. This condition results from deficiency of C1 inhibitor. Which of the following best explains the pathophysiology?
o: Uncontrolled activation of the membrane attack complex causing cell lysis
Excessive C3a and C5a production leading to mast cell degranulation and edema
Deficient opsonization resulting in persistent bacterial infections and fever
Impaired phagocytosis allowing accumulation of circulating immune complexes
Loss of selectin-mediated leukocyte rolling causing defective neutrophil recruitment
qs.e: C1 inhibitor (C1 INH) is a key regulatory protein that blocks activation of C1, the first protein of the classical complement pathway. Without it, there's uncontrolled complement activation producing excessive amounts of C3a and C5a - the anaphylatoxins. These fragments stimulate mast cell degranulation and histamine release, causing the vasodilation and increased vascular permeability that leads to angioedema (swell

qs.q: A 30-year-old woman with selective IgA deficiency receives a blood transfusion and immediately develops urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm, and hypotension. Her temperature is normal. Most likely transfusion reaction?
qs.e: IgA deficiency + anti-IgA antibodies + immediate allergic reaction with urticaria, bronchospasm, hypotension = anaphylactic transfusion reaction. IgA-deficient patients form anti-IgA antibodies and react severely when exposed to IgA in transfused blood products.

exam: What immediate steps do you take for a patient with rapidly expanding tongue swelling? — Assess airway, give high‑flow O₂, prepare for intubation, give IM adrenaline if anaphylaxis suspected.

How would you differentiate histamine‑mediated from bradykinin‑mediated angioedema at the bedside? — Look for urticaria, recent allergen exposure, and ACE‑I use; absence of itching and ACE‑I history suggest bradykinin type.

A patient on lisinopril develops lip swelling without urticaria. What is the next best management? — Discontinue lisinopril, monitor airway, give icatibant or fresh frozen plasma if airway threatened; avoid antihistamines as primary therapy.
What laboratory test helps confirm hereditary angioedema and what result is expected? — Serum C4; low level during attacks and remission.
Why is fresh frozen plasma useful in acute hereditary angioedema when specific C1‑INH concentrate is unavailable? — It supplies functional C1‑INH, reducing bradykinin production.

A patient presents with swollen eyelids and a fever. How do you rule out cellulitis? — Look for erythema, warmth, tenderness, systemic signs; obtain CBC and consider empiric antibiotics if infection likely.
What are the contraindications for using epinephrine in angioedema? — None in life‑threatening airway edema; caution in severe coronary disease but airway takes priority.

Explain how traditional herbal remedies can precipitate angioedema in this setting. — Unknown allergens or contaminants can trigger mast‑cell degranulation; always obtain a thorough medication history.
ai.title: Angioedema
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Angioedema is sudden, deep swelling of the skin and mucosa caused by increased vascular permeability. It can be life‑threatening when the airway is involved. Management hinges on rapid assessment, treating the trigger, and securing the airway.

b: Deep, non‑pitting swelling of lips, eyelids, tongue, genitalia, or extremities
Absence of primary wheal (distinguishes from urticaria)
Rapid onset (minutes to hours)
sections.p: Angioedema is a transient, non‑pitting edema of the deep dermis, subcutaneous tissue, or mucosa, usually lasting <72 h. Diagnosis is clinical; look for swelling without urticaria and assess airway risk.

b: Mild: localized swelling, no airway compromise
Moderate: extensive facial/oropharyngeal swelling, mild dysphagia
Severe: progressive tongue or laryngeal edema, stridor, voice change
sections.p: Severity is graded by airway involvement and extent of swelling. Staging guides urgency of airway protection.

b: Histamine‑mediated: foods, insect stings, drugs (penicillins, NSAIDs)
Bradykinin‑mediated: ACE‑inhibitors, ARBs, hereditary C1‑INH deficiency
Infections: HIV‑related lymphadenopathy, TB drug reactions, malaria‑related drug hypersensitivity
Herbal remedies & traditional medicines containing unknown allergens
sections.p: Identify the trigger; categorize as histamine‑mediated, bradykinin‑mediated, or idiopathic. In low‑resource East African settings, common triggers differ from high‑income countries.

b: Swelling is firm, non‑pitting, may be painful
No itching unless urticaria co‑exists
Possible abdominal pain if visceral edema (rare)
Voice change, drooling, difficulty swallowing in oropharyngeal involvement
sections.p: Patients report sudden swelling of lips, eyes, tongue, or genitalia, often after exposure to a trigger. Respiratory distress signals airway involvement.
Investigations aim to confirm the mechanism and rule out mimics; many are unavailable in low‑resource settings, so clinical judgment is paramount.

t.b: Distinguishes hereditary/bradykinin angioedema (low C4) from histamine type (normal) — if unavailable, rely on drug history and family history
Confirms hereditary or acquired C1‑INH deficiency — if unavailable, consider recurrent, ACE‑I‑unrelated episodes
Detect eosinophilia (suggests allergic cause) or infection‑related drug reaction
Look for soft‑tissue swelling of the neck; if unavailable, assess clinically for stridor and use bedside laryngoscopy if possible

b: Stridor, voice hoarseness, or inability to speak
Drooling, dysphagia, or inability to swallow saliva
Rapidly expanding neck swelling
Hypotension or tachycardia suggesting anaphylactic shock
sections.p: Airway obstruction is the most urgent threat. Secondary complications include aspiration, hypoxia, and shock in anaphylaxis.

b: Stop the offending drug immediately (ACE‑I, NSAID, etc.)
Airway: position patient upright, give high‑flow oxygen, prepare for intubation or surgical airway
Bradykinin‑mediated: give icatibant (if available) or fresh frozen plasma (provides C1‑INH) – avoid antihistamines as they are ineffective
Supportive: IV fluids for hypotension, monitor vitals every 15 min
sections.p: Treat the underlying trigger, secure the airway, and give targeted pharmacotherapy. In low‑resource settings, use readily available drugs and early transfer if airway cannot be protected.

b: Document trigger and educate patient/family
If ACE‑I related, switch to alternative antihypertensive (e.g., calcium channel blocker)
For hereditary C1‑INH deficiency, arrange referral for prophylactic C1‑INH concentrate or lanadelumab where possible
Provide emergency self‑injectable icatibant or plasma-derived C1‑INH for known bradykinin cases
sections.p: Long‑term planning prevents recurrence and reduces mortality.

b: Urticaria – superficial wheals, intense itching, rapid resolution
Cellulitis – painful, erythematous, warm, often febrile, responds to antibiotics
Lymphedema – chronic, non‑painful, non‑fluctuating, usually lower limbs
sections.p: Distinguish angioedema from other swelling disorders.

b: Normal C4 does not exclude hereditary angioedema during remission
Eosinophil count may be normal in drug‑induced histamine angioedema
sections.p: Certain labs may be normal despite serious disease.

whenToSeekHelp: Progressive tongue or neck swelling, stridor, voice change, or inability to swallow
Hypotension, tachycardia, or collapse suggesting anaphylactic shock
